summary:
This L0009 run was started by the line's timer, not by an instruction. So there were no 'Asked' items, and the empty answers list is right. It made no claims and registered no experiments. It continued building moving stacks (spheres resting on spheres that ride the plate) on branch method/rest. The stacks are still outside the event loop.

Everything in evidence/L0009-build-2026-11-25-3.json that I reran reproduced in a fresh clone of commit e299265. The method tests gave 52 passed. The frozen engine tests, run with the method off, gave 74 passed. The offline stall replay matched to the last digit: the stack ran 0.3964654852972904 time units, ended when the top contact opened, and its books closed to 2.6e-14.

I also ran the roll-off cases on the code from before the dip search (bcd1d5f) and from after it (4431b64, e299265). Event times and final states were identical bit for bit. The force solves were the same (1848 and 1701), and the dip search added 1470 and 1316 event evaluations. So the claim that the dip search acted on every step but never fired on these cases is confirmed. That answers the missed-dip point from my review of 2026-11-24, as a sampling test (not a bound), which decision D0081 states honestly. The pytest scratch point from my last two reviews is fixed: no new pytest folders appeared in ~/.tmp after 09:46.

One new problem, which matters for the next step (wiring stacks into the loop). The stack integrator accepts a contact marked 'rolling' that is actually slipping. It then holds that slip constant and books friction work on it. In the session's own stall replay, the lower sphere (the plate rider) starts as 'rolling' on the plate with a horizontal slip of 0.0171. That is not round-off: the plate ride lets riders slide. The slip stays exactly 0.0171 for the whole 0.40 time units. I split the friction loss by contact. That contact supplies 0.0032 of the reported 0.0295 friction loss, about one ninth, and the top contact supplies the other 0.0263. Coulomb's law would have that contact slide, with friction mu N against the slip, until the slip reached zero.

The books still close, because that friction work is counted. That is the caveat from my last review come true: closed books show the integration is consistent, not that the motion is right. Here the energy happened to be lost, but the sign of friction work on a contact held at a constant slip is not guaranteed, so in general it could be a gain. Decision D0083 made the start check refuse a rolling contact that needs more than mu N. It does not refuse a rolling contact that has slip. A start check (or a hand-off from the ride that carries the rider's sliding mode) is needed before stacks go into the loop.

The line's new state says the stalled pair 'moved smoothly for 0.40 time units ... with energy books closing to 3e-14'. That is literally true, but the lower contact was not modelled correctly during that motion, and the state should say so.

At neighbouring conditions I ran the same replay. With seed 2 at f* 0.3, the layer also stalls in cycle 0, at local time 5.826, on a rider and a sphere on top of it at 29 degrees from vertical. Both contacts there start with slip at round-off, about 1e-8 or less. The stack ran 0.75 time units until the top contact began to slide, with books closing to 9e-14 and friction loss of 4e-9. That is a clean case. With seed 1 at f* 0.4, the stall is at local time 4.978, on a similar pair. There the top contact starts as 'rolling' with a slip of 0.0044, the same defect. That run went 0.83 time units until the top contact slid, with books closing to 3e-13. So the replay result is not a one-off, and neither is the slip problem: two of the three stalls I looked at hand the stack a slipping contact labelled rolling.

Smaller points. The replay script removes a residual approach speed of 1.2e-8 from the top sphere before the stack starts, outside the books. That is negligible offline, but it must be booked once it happens inside the engine. The recorded end time of 10:53:00 is again a forecast: the final commit was at 10:51:48. program check passes; it failed only on my own scratch, which I removed. The latest approval is from 2026-11-24 03:19 UTC, more than a day old. The question to Chris (does an integrated moving stack count as time-stepping?) is still open and honestly framed.

run_conditions.assessment: The run started at 10:38:01 UTC, one second after its scheduled time, and committed its records at 10:51:48 UTC, about fourteen minutes later and well within its limit. It ran on a Linux worker, so there is no Mac sleep log to check. The work was building code plus short single-threaded checks. My reruns of those checks took 25 to 55 seconds each, so the recorded 0.12 CPU hours, a sum of wall times as the summary says, is plausible. No jobs are in flight: active.jsonl is empty. The scratch folder is empty. The data folder is about 0.7 gigabytes of the 15 allowed, and 90 gigabytes are free against a floor of 40. The load average at the time of this check was about 9 to 16 on 40 cores. The machine did not limit the science. Waiting are stage three, moving stacks in the event loop (the next timer run), and Chris's answer to the time-stepping question.
discrepancies: The summary records the end as 10:53:00Z, but the final commit was at 10:51:48Z. The end time is a forecast, not a measurement, as in the two previous runs.
The CPU figure of 0.12 hours is a sum of wall times, not read from ps or logs. The summary says so openly. It is a small departure from CLAUDE.md's 'not an estimate'.
Fixed since last review: pytest's scratch now goes under sequel-data/tmp. No new folders appeared in ~/.tmp/pytest-of-roborobo after 09:46.
